content: The Black Locust, scientifically known as Robinia pseudoacacia, is a tree belonging to the subfamily Faboideae within the pea family Fabaceae. It is native to the southeastern United States but has been extensively planted and naturalized in other temperate regions of North America, Europe, and Asia. In some areas, it is considered an invasive species. A less common name for this tree is False Acacia, which is a direct translation of its specific epithet. The tree was introduced to Britain in 1636. The Black Locust can grow to a height of 70 feet, with a trunk diameter of 3 to 4 feet in mature specimens. The bark is thick, deeply furrowed, and dark gray-brown with reddish tinges. The branches are brittle and form an oblong, narrow crown. The tree spreads through underground shoots. Its leaves are compound, odd-pinnate, and range from 8 to 14 inches in length. Each leaf typically has 7 to 9 leaflets, which are 1 to 2 inches long and 0.5 to 0.75 inches wide. The leaflets are dull dark green on the upper surface and paler beneath, turning a clear pale yellow in autumn. The leaves fold together in wet weather and at night, a characteristic shared by many members of the legume family. The flowers of the Black Locust are intensely fragrant, white, and borne in pendulous racemes 8 to 20 cm long. They are papilionaceous, nectar-bearing, and bloom in May after the leaves have emerged. The flowers are considered edible. The fruit is a legume, 5 to 10 cm long, containing 4 to 10 seeds. The seeds are dark orange-brown with irregular markings. The pods ripen in late autumn and often remain on the branches until early spring. Unlike the Honey Locust, the Black Locust lacks long branched spines on its trunk, instead having pairs of short thorns at the base of each leaf. The wood of the Black Locust is pale yellowish-brown, heavy, hard, strong, and close-grained. It is highly durable when in contact with the ground, making it valuable for fence posts and small watercraft. The heartwood contains flavonoids that allow it to resist rot and last over 100 years in soil. In Europe, particularly in the Netherlands, the Black Locust is promoted as a sustainable alternative to tropical hardwoods due to its rot resistance. However, the wood should be split when green and dried for 2 to 3 years before use. It is one of the heaviest and hardest woods in North America. The Black Locust is a major honey plant in the eastern United States and is the source of the renowned acacia monofloral honey in France. It is often planted along streets and in parks in Europe due to its tolerance of pollution. However, it is unsuitable for small gardens because of its large size and rapid growth. The cultivar 'Frisia,' with bright yellow-green leaves, is occasionally used as an ornamental tree. The tree has nitrogen-fixing bacteria on its root system, enabling it to grow in poor soils and colonize disturbed areas. Despite its many uses, the Black Locust is susceptible to damage from borers, which can riddle the trunk and branches, significantly reducing its value as a timber tree in many parts of the United States. Young trees grow quickly and vigorously but often become stunted and diseased, rarely living long enough to attain commercial value. The Black Locust reproduces through its distinctive hanging pods, which are smaller and lighter than those of the Honey Locust and can be carried long distances by the wind. However, unlike the Honey Locust, the pods of the Black Locust are toxic, as are most parts of the tree, especially the bark. The flowers are the only exception and are not toxic. Some reports suggest that the seeds and young pods may be edible when cooked, as heat decomposes the plant's toxins. Horses that consume the plant may exhibit symptoms such as anorexia, depression, diarrhea, colic, weakness, and cardiac arrhythmia. Symptoms typically appear about one hour after ingestion, and immediate veterinary attention is required. The name locust is believed to have been given to Robinia by Jesuit missionaries, who thought it was the tree that supported St. John in the wilderness. However, the Black Locust is native only to North America. The true locust tree of the New Testament is thought to be the locust tree of Spain, which is also native to Syria. Fossil evidence suggests that Robinia traces back to the Eocene and Miocene periods in Europe.
